items.title: U.S. aviation regulator approves long-delayed 737 Max 10 for service
items.description: Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Boeing 737 MAX 10 performs a demonstration flight during the Paris Air Show in Le Bourget, north of Paris, France, June 19, 2023. (AP Photo/Lewis Joly, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Lewis Joly</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines.
items.body:
Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.

The 737 Max 10’s certification represents another milestone in Boeing’s efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed “extensive safety reviews,” including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing.

“To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago,” Duffy said during a visit to Boeing’s manufacturing plant Tuesday in Everett, Washington.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The Max 10 is an important piece of the company’s effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face.

Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy’s visit that the certification “clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation.” The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8.

“Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many,” Pope said. “It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth.”

The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027.

The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification.

Boeing’s struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing’s manufacturing and safety practices.

The delays have held up a key part of Boeing’s business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more.

The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus’s A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10.

Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft -- a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses.

Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10’s design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers.

The Max 10’s certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August.

Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company’s resilience.

In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

Josh Funk and Rio Yamat, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said it’s ‘time to move forward’ after the province voted against separation in Monday’s referendum.
items.body:
Albertans rejected holding a second referendum to separate as voters overwhelmingly chose to stay in Canada, CTV News projects.

In a historic vote that saw the oil-rich province put the question of separation to the public, roughly 75 per cent of voters thought Alberta should stay in Canada, while just under 25 per cent voted to pursue a binding referendum on leaving, according to preliminary results just after 8 a.m. MT.

  • LIVE: Real-time data. Interactive maps. Every question. Every result.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says as long as she is premier, she will not call a second referendum on the question of separation.

The premier put the matter to rest in a televised update at 6:45 p.m. MT while urging separatists to give Ottawa another chance.

The remaining nine questions, focused largely on immigration and constitutional changes, are also being counted right now and some have close races.

The emphatic result to remain culminates a year-long campaign from pro-Canada and separatist groups.

The Alberta government, on the other hand, campaigned for yes votes on the first nine questions, and Smith also advocated for the province to remain in Canada.

Elections Alberta was expected to announce results for Question 10 by 4 a.m. MT, but not all polls are reporting results yet.

Results for the first nine questions will be announced Wednesday morning.

items.title: U.S. food importer sues Trump over Canada tariffs
items.description: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump and a Canadian flag are seen in this composite image (AP Photo/Alex Brandon; The Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.
items.body:
WASHINGTON – An American food importer filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration over Washington’s latest tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, claiming U.S. President Donald Trump has overstepped the power of his office.

The Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business based in New Jersey and has imported Canadian cheese for around 100 years. The company said Trump’s use of a depression-era trade law to enact tariffs on Canadian dairy will cost them US$40 million a year.

The lawsuit was filed Tuesday by Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert Global Group in a New York-based court. Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht told CTV News she’s played “a game of whack-a-mole” with Trump’s tariffs.

“We will continue to keep fighting these things as long as they are abusing the (U.S.) Constitution as it’s written, and abusing the separation of powers, and basically taking authority that the executive branch doesn’t have,” Albrecht said.

In a separate news release shared Tuesday, Albrecht said: “No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits of (the U.S.) Congress required.”

After trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down in August, Trump used the little-known Tariff Act of 1930 to impose more punishment on Canadian imports, including dairy, alcohol, furniture and yes, even hockey sticks.

“Section 338 is from the Trade Act of 1930, the Smoot-Hawley Trade Act, which kind of launched the Great Depression, so, not something we’d really want to emulate. The section has never been used before to implement tariffs on American importers,” Albrecht told CTV News.

Thomas Gellert, co-CEO of Gellert Global Group, said in a news release the company has “spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry.”

“These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain,” Gellert said.

This is just the latest legal challenge to how far the U.S. president can go with his tariff policies. The lawsuit asked the court to declare these tariffs unlawful and order a refund ... with interest.

While neither Trump nor the White House have publicly commented on the lawsuit, a Trump administration told The Canadian Press on background that the president’s actions will be vigorously defended in court.

With files from The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The bank says Darrel Hackett will retire from his role as U.S. CEO after more than 22 years with BMO and will transition to an executive vice-chair and senior adviser role effective Nov. 1.
items.body:
BMO announced a leadership transition for the head of its U.S. operations.

The bank says Darrel Hackett will retire from his role as U.S. CEO after more than 22 years with BMO and will transition to an executive vice-chair and senior adviser role effective Nov. 1.

BMO says Tim Cox has been appointed, effective Nov. 1, as the U.S. country head of BMO Financial Group and the CEO of its U.S. subsidiaries BMO Financial Corp. and BMO Bank N.A.

Cox joined the bank in 2010 and has held various legal and regulatory compliance roles.

Darryl White, BMO CEO, says in a news release that Hackett played a role in helping build the U.S. business.

The announcement comes after BMO, TD Bank and other large U.S. lenders were identified in a report by the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency about debanking and limiting access to financial services for certain U.S. customers due to their political beliefs.

items.title: Italy’s pasta production has ‘ground to a halt, or is close to,’ as truck drivers protest over fuel prices
items.description: The production of Italian pasta is under threat as a protest by truck drivers in the south of the country over soaring fuel prices and the cost of living blocks deliveries to factories.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Packages of imported Italian pasta sit on shelves Tuesday, Nov. 11, 2025, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Ryan Sun)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Ryan Sun</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The production of Italian pasta is under threat as a protest by truck drivers in the south of the country over soaring fuel prices and the cost of living blocks deliveries to factories.
items.body:
MILAN -- The production of Italian pasta is under threat as a protest by truck drivers in the south of the country over soaring fuel prices and the cost of living blocks deliveries to factories.

There are also growing concerns about food supplies in Rome, as transport bottlenecks hamper deliveries from southern Italy to the capital.

Italian agriculture lobby group Confagricoltura warned that producers in Sicily would have to destroy large quantities of perishable products if transportation did not resume.

Pasta maker Rummo, based in the Campania region, said on Tuesday it had suspended production after running out of ingredients.

Almost all major pasta producers in the neighboring region of Puglia, which together with Campania and Sicily form the heartland of Italy’s pasta production, are facing similar difficulties, CEO Cosimo Rummo told daily la Repubblica.

“This means that most of Italy’s pasta production has ground to a halt, or is close to,” he said.

La Molisana, another producer based in the Molise region, said it had experienced a significant drop in production and had been forced to draw on its stocks of raw materials such as wheat and semola flour.

Italy’s pasta supply chain last year generated €13.5 billion in revenue, the European House-Ambrosetti (TEHA Group) said in a report in September.

The Centro Agroalimentare Roma (CAR), Italy’s largest wholesale fruit and vegetable market, said roadblocks and higher transport costs were causing shortages of products such as tomatoes, peppers and grapes, pushing up prices and increasing reliance on imports from countries including Spain and Albania.

Food, petrol running out

The government is pledging more aid for road hauliers. After meeting with their representatives on Tuesday, Deputy Infrastructure Minister Edoardo Rixi said a package worth more than €150 million would be made available soon.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s administration is also preparing a security crackdown in response to weekend riots in Milan and other northern cities, which developed on the back of demonstrations against inflation.

Vincenzo Aleccia, president of the Trapani trucking consortium in the western Sicilian port city, told Reuters that he knew the disruption was enormous but added that “it’s a peaceful protest and it’s for the benefit of the people,” saying rising prices affected everyone.

The protest, which began last week with the blocking of roads, motorways and ports in Sicily and the south, is causing shortages at supermarkets and queues at petrol stations.

“People were trying to grab whatever was left. I had to go to a nearby town, and I also stocked up on flour and the food we consume most,” said Zineb Boutimah, 45, who lives in Locri, a town in the southern province of Reggio Calabria.

Elena Lombardo, 78, also from Locri, said her local petrol station attendant had urged her to fill up her tank on Monday, warning, “I don’t know whether there will be any petrol tomorrow.”

On Tuesday, the petrol station was closed.

(Reporting by Sara Rossi and Francesca Piscioneri; Editing by Alvise Armellini and Keith Weir)

items.title: Carnival Cruise Lines introduces dynamic pricing model
items.description: The price is about to rise for some travellers who want to vacation on the high seas. One of the world’s largest cruise companies, Carnival Cruise Lines, will introduce dynamic pricing for certain onboard packages starting on Dec. 1.

items._ogDesc: The price is about to rise for some travellers who want to vacation on the high seas. One of the world’s largest cruise companies, Carnival Cruise Lines, will introduce dynamic pricing for certain onboard packages starting on Dec. 1.
items.body:
The price is about to rise for some travellers who want to vacation on the high seas.

Carnival Cruise Lines, one of the world’s largest cruise companies, will introduce dynamic pricing for certain onboard packages starting on Dec. 1.

The cruise line announced the introduction of dynamic pricing in a news release about its new packaging framework, called FunPacks. The company called the new structure its “largest offering of packages tailored to different vacation styles.”

However, the prices for certain onboard packages are up in the air. The statement read.

“Carnival will also introduce dynamic pricing for beverage packages and Wi-Fi plans,” the company said. “Pricing will vary based on sailing length, itinerary and season.”

Carnival said the new dynamic pricing model will apply to Wi-Fi and beverage plans in bundled FunPacks and those purchased on their own.

What is dynamic pricing?

Also known as surge pricing, dynamic pricing is a strategy where businesses push up prices at times of high demand. This is commonly seen in airline ticket prices and hotel room rates during holiday seasons, as well as Uber surge pricing during peak hours.

According to a 2024 report written by Kate Gibson for Harvard Business School, “Dynamic pricing is a strategy that bases products or services’ prices on evolving market trends.”

Dynamic pricing has frustrated customers in the past. Recent examples include music fans hoping to score a concert ticket, only to find the prices had been hiked due to high demand.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

In this case, it may be cruise ship passengers sinking deeper into their wallets to maximize Carnival Cruise Lines’ revenues.

In an email to CTV News, a representative from Carnival said dynamic pricing for individual beverage and Wi-Fi packages “allows us to better align pricing with the type of cruise a guest books while providing greater flexibility and reflecting seasonal demand.”

“Importantly, once a guest purchases a package, their confirmed price is locked in and will not change even if pricing is adjusted later,” the statement read.

With files from CTV News’ Elianna Lev

items._ogDesc: SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications operations and its business of leasing computing power to other companies boomed.
items.body:
NEW YORK — SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications operations and its business of leasing computing power to other companies boomed.

The company, run by Elon Musk, posted net income in the three months through September of US$4.4 billion, or 35 cents per share. That’s more than double what Wall Street expected, and reverses a loss from the year-earlier period. Revenue soared to US$14.6 billion, up 161 per cent.

“They beat across all metrics and the Starlink business looks to be accelerating,” said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, adding about investors. “This is just what the Street wanted.”

The newly public company’s results marked a sharp break from more than a year of losses.

The stock rose 4.6 per cent in after-hours trading.

In an investor call, Musk said that for next month’s launch of its Starship rocket, SpaceX will attempt to grab both the booster and ship with mechanical arms upon return to base, a key step toward demonstrating it can reuse the massive spacecraft.

“The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle,” Musk said, calling the attempt, if successful, “a massive technology milestone.”

SpaceX hopes to get Starship on a regular launch pattern in preparation for NASA’s upcoming lunar missions.

The company already has huge contracts with the federal government, and House Democrats have called for investigations into those contracts and Musk’s work with the Department of Government Efficiency. Musk has spent US$276 million since July in support of Republican candidates.

He recently drew criticism from politicians in Washington after speeds for a military version of SpaceX’s satellite communications service were slowed for Ukraine following President Donald Trump’s deal to get more diesel oil from Russia amid a push to end the war. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that it was Musk who ordered the slowdown, impeding Ukraine’s use of drones along the front. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Journal story.

Both Trump and Musk have denied responsibility for the slowdown.

As midterm elections near, Musk on Monday promised to give one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year, though he provided no details on how the distribution would be carried out. With communities nationwide protesting the construction of large data centers and concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence, AI companies are trying to build some goodwill. Anthropic pledged to commit five per cent of its shares to a new “public benefit” fund.

In a filing for its initial public offering in June, SpaceX warned that a change in control of Congress could have a “material and adverse impact on our growth and competitive position.”

SpaceX shares have been under pressure over concerns that the company was spending too much on major projects to compete with rivals such as Anthropic. The company said capital expenditures totaled US$19.6 billion last quarter, nearly triple the figure from a year earlier, and it forecast spending would grow to US$35 billion to US$40 billion in the current quarter.

Shares of SpaceX closed Tuesday at US$147.79, down from a peak near US$201 after its IPO, which made Musk the world’s first trillionaire at the time. But the share prices for SpaceX and Tesla have since dropped, reducing his net worth to US$925 billion, according to Forbes magazine.

Bernard Condon, The Associated Press

items.title: ‘We’re going to take care of Bombardier’: Trump backs down on threat against Canadian jet maker
items.description: Donald Trump appears to be backing away from his threat to shut Canadian aerospace giant Bombardier out of the U.S. market, after learning about the company’s significant operations in Kansas.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump and jet planes are assembled at Bombardier's aircraft assembly centre in Mississauga in a combination photo. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin/THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sammy Kogan)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Donald Trump appears to be backing away from his threat to shut Canadian aerospace giant Bombardier out of the U.S. market, after learning about the company’s significant operations in Kansas.
items.body:
OTTAWA – U.S. President Donald Trump appears to be backing away from his threat to shut Canadian aerospace giant Bombardier out of the U.S. market, after learning about the company’s significant operations in Kansas.

In September, Trump threatened to block sales of Bombardier jets in the United States amid a growing trade dispute with Canada.

“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 7. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’”

But while visiting Kansas on Monday, Trump struck a dramatically different tone after learning about Bombardier’s operations in Wichita, where the company employs about 1,500 people.

“We’re going to take care of Bombardier,” Trump told 12 News in Kansas. He repeated the sentiment on stage at a rally later in the day.

“I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away … I’ll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company,” Trump said. “But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So, we’ll take care of those people and the jobs.”

Dominic LeBlanc, the federal minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, has argued for months that Bombardier is deeply embedded in the American economy.

“Bombardier has many hundreds and thousands of employees in the United States and has had for a long time. I had seen a number of legislators in the United States, including Republicans, express concerns this summer when President Trump had made those comments about Bombardier,” said Leblanc.

Trump was in Kansas to campaign for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is locked in an unusually competitive re-election fight against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Kansas has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, but polls have shown a close race this year.

Trump’s September threat against Bombardier had become a political issue in Kansas because of the company’s 1,500 jobs in Wichita. Marshall was among the Kansas lawmakers who contacted the White House after Trump threatened to block Bombardier from the U.S. market.

Trump specifically cited Marshall’s involvement when he told local television Monday that his administration would “take care of Bombardier.”

Bombardier employs about 3,500 people across the United States, with more than 40 per cent of those jobs in Wichita. The company last week announced a US$50-million investment in Wichita, home to its U.S. and defence headquarters.

“We’re going to find a deal with the United States at some point that’s in the interest of the entire Canadian economy,” said Leblanc.

items.title: Major projects bill would put decades of labour stability at risk: union leader
items.description: Proposed amendments to Canada’s labour code outlined in Bill C-39 could put decades of labour stability at risk, Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske told a parliamentary committee.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, prepares to appear before the legislative committee on Bill C-39 in the Parliamentary Precinct in Ottawa on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Proposed amendments to Canada’s labour code outlined in Bill C-39 could put decades of labour stability at risk, Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske told a parliamentary committee.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Proposed amendments to Canada’s labour code outlined in Bill C-39 could put decades of labour stability at risk, Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday.

The 243-page bill seeks to fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

The bill also proposes changes to Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to state that a minister can order a business under federal jurisdiction to resume operations, or put parties into binding arbitration.

Bruske told MPs on the special House of Commons committee struck to review the bill that those proposed new powers effectively eliminate the right to strike.

“What looks like greater stability on paper is going to create more instability,” she told members of Parliament at the committee meeting.

Canadian Union of Public Employees national president Mark Hancock told the committee that when companies know the government will bail them out during a strike, they won’t put their best offers forward in contract negotiations.

“Bill C-39 doesn’t encourage employers to bargain,” he said. “It encourages them to lowball workers and wait for the minister to do their dirty work.”

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu defended the legislation at a meeting of the C-39 committee on Monday.

Hajdu said the bill strengthens the right to strike by removing the ability to use Section 107 before a labour disruption. She argued the government has a responsibility to act during an “exceptionally consequential” dispute.

“Protecting workers and protecting the national interest go hand in hand,” she said.

The Canadian Labour Congress has proposed amendments that would ensure Section 107 does not give the minister the power to end legal strikes. Bruske said the group also has proposed striking an independent panel of experts to assess whether ongoing strikes have created a genuine national economic emergency.

“The panel would advise government, and if intervention were necessary, government would have to introduce legislation and make its case in Parliament,” she said.

Through C-39, the Liberals are proposing to introduce a new special mediator position. The special mediator would document both sides’ arguments in a labour dispute and publish a report to identify sticking points before talks break down.

It’s a tool the government sees being used in cases where unions and employers have a history of acrimony.

If passed, C-39 would require the jobs minister to consider the special mediator’s report before triggering Section 107. The minister must also conclude that the labour disruption is adversely affecting the “national interest” before taking the extraordinary step of ending a strike.

Bruske said her organization has proposed that special mediators be independent of government.

“Our experience under the Public Service Labor Relations Act raises some concerns that the proposed special mediator process could delay settlements rather than help achieve them,” she said.

The Liberals have used Section 107 numerous times in recent years leaned to end strikes in federally regulated sectors such as rail, ports and air transportation.

Labour experts have said the new language in C-39 likely does confer additional powers on the minister -- and those powers will be subject to Charter challenges questioning their constitutionality.

A Charter statement for the bill says the changes around Section 107 may potentially engage section 2(d) of the Charter -- the freedom of association.

It says a ministerial direction to the Canada Industrial Relations Board to order employees to resume their duties, extend a collective agreement, or impose a binding method of resolving outstanding issues, may engage the right to strike.

“The amendments would not generally prohibit strikes or lockouts. Rather, the proposed authority could be exercised when a strike or lockout is already underway and would be subject to specified conditions,” says the statement. “These considerations constrain the circumstances in which the authority may be exercised.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: Albertans have voted ‘yes’ to referendum questions on immigration. Here’s how Carney responded.
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal and provincial governments should work together to get immigration down to sustainable levels before Alberta takes steps to change the Constitution to do so itself.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney takes questions from journalists as he arrives for a meeting of the federal cabinet on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal and provincial governments should work together to get immigration down to sustainable levels before Alberta takes steps to change the Constitution to do so itself.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal and provincial governments should work together to get immigration down to sustainable levels before Alberta takes steps to do so on its own.

Albertans cast their ballots on a slate of referendum questions Monday, and while the question around separation drew the most attention, there were nine others that cover a range of issues, from proposed Constitutional changes to health-care access.

Five of the questions outside of the one on separation were focused on immigration, and could require constitutional changes to implement.

“This government has recognized from the start, the need to take back control on immigration, and we’ve done so,” Carney told reporters on Parliament Hill Tuesday morning, while answering questions about the Alberta referendum results.

“I believe, for example, on the issue of immigration and co-operation between the federal government and the provinces for a sustainable immigration system that works for Canadians, works for our economy, works for our society, and treats those who come to our country, choose to come to our country, with the dignity and standards that they deserve, that we can accomplish that without constitutional change,” Carney also said.

On the question of whether the provincial government should have more control over who comes into the province, according to preliminary results, Albertans have voted “yes.”

Asked whether the province should pass a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta­-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs — such as health care, education and other social services — Albertans voted “yes.”

Another question proposed making temporary residents wait a year before accessing certain social supports. Albertans voted “yes” to that referendum question, along with a question that asked whether individuals with non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta should have to pay fees to access public health care and education.

Carney said he spoke with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith Tuesday morning, firstly about additional support for the victims and families of the deadly fire at the Canadian Forces Base in Wainwright, Alta.

“That was our first focus, and then we turned to the referendum and moving forward in the spirit of co-operative federalism, including on issues of immigration, other common priorities of the federal government, the provinces, but underlying it, priorities of Canadians,” Carney said.

Canada-Alberta ‘already engaged’ on immigration: Minister

In an interview on CTV Question Period last week, meanwhile, the Liberals’ only cabinet minister from Alberta signalled an openness on Ottawa’s behalf to engage in discussions with the province on enhanced autonomy over immigration levels.

“I can tell you that we are already engaged in those discussions, and (Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday) we didn’t really need a referendum to tell us what issues we need to talk about with Alberta or any other province,” Eleanor Olszewski told host Vassy Kapelos.

When Kapelos pressed her on whether that will mean more provincial autonomy over immigration, Olszewski said, “it’s a shared jurisdiction, and we are engaged in discussions with the province with respect to levels and sustainability.”

Federal immigration Minister Lena Diab also alluded to working with Alberta when it comes to immigration when asked directly if the federal government is prepared to give the province more immigration powers.

“I recognize the significance of co-operations between the provinces and the federal government when it comes to immigration,” Diab said on Friday at a press conference in Kitchener, Ont. “It is a joint provincial-federal responsibility, and we will continue to work jointly with all provinces and territories across this country to make sure that we have the best immigration system in the world.”

Budget committed to lowering immigration

Immigration levels in Canada reached a record high in 2024. According to the federal government, 483,640 immigrants were admitted as permanent residents that year, which was in line with targets set out in the Government of Canada’s Immigration Levels Plan at the time. In 2025, that number dropped to about 393,500 new permanent residents.

In Carney’s first budget in late 2025, the Liberals set new targets, promising to “responsibly manage immigration to alleviate pressures on housing demand.”

“The 2026–2028 Immigration Levels Plan will return immigration to sustainable levels by stabilising new permanent resident admissions at less than one per cent of the Canadian population beyond 2027 and reducing the total number of temporary residents to less than five per cent of the population by the end of 2027, down from a peak of 7.6 per cent in 2024,” the budget stated.

But in an interview with The New York Times in September, Carney said Canada will eventually resume a “controlled increase” in its population once the immigration system remains fully under control. The prime minister did not elaborate further on what that increase would look like or when it could happen.

Asked on Friday about why immigration could soon be adjusted, Diab pointed to the country’s slow population growth and the federal government’s “ambitious agenda.”

“We are going to want to drive growth. We do need people,” Diab said.

Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the number of asylum seekers is down by 70 per cent, temporary foreign workers by 60 per cent, and foreign students by 80 per cent, over the last year and a half.

“I’m not saying that that stabilization is complete, but where we go from here needs to be established in co-operation with the provinces, and that’s very much the spirit of at least one of the (referendum) questions,” he also said.

The federal government’s updated immigration level plan will be released in November.

Poilievre agrees with Alberta votes

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre — who represents a rural Alberta riding — said he supports Albertans’ decisions with regards to immigration and “bringing (it) back under control.”

“The provinces should have control in selection and numbers because they have to provide the services, regulate the job market, and the housing for people who come in,” he said. “And taxpayers should not be forced to pay deluxe benefits to people who are here illegally.”

“The prime minister was wrong on this, and he’s been wrong on immigration all along,” he added.

In an interview with CTV News senior political correspondent Mike Le Couteur on Tuesday, immigration lawyer Chantal Desloges said greater powers for the provinces on immigration could impede the federal government’s ability to make decision that are national in scope.

She also said that because the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms protects the right to mobility — outlined in section six of the Charter — it could infringe on the rights of immigrants who become permanent residents to then restrict where they can and cannot live in Canada.

“Constitutionally, immigration is a federal power, and the feds share that power with the provinces through a variety of different sort of arrangements that they have with each other,” Desloges explained. “The federal government has to look at immigration from a national perspective, and thinking about demographics, thinking about things that are in the national interest.”

“If all of the provinces and territories start having their own little piece of the pie, where they all have a say in who’s going where and who’s doing what, that really limits the federal government in terms of the long-range national planning that they can actually do,” she added.

items._ogDesc: The PBO projects Canada's federal borrowing will outpace deficits 2-to-1, with debt servicing costs exploding to consume 1 in 7 revenue dollars by 2030.
items.body:
Is it a bird? A plane? No, it’s… the size of Canada’s debt servicing costs. The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s (PBO) latest Economic and Fiscal Outlook projects Ottawa will accumulate $333 billion in deficit spending over 5 years. However, the Government of Canada (GoC) will need to borrow nearly three-quarters of a trillion dollars. Debt servicing is now the fastest-growing federal expense, projected to consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030.

Federal Borrowing To Grow More Than 2x As Much As Deficits

Ottawa will accumulate $333.3 billion in cumulative deficits from 2026-27 through 2030-31. At the same time, the GoC will borrow an additional $732.9 billion, according to the PBO’s projections. That’s roughly 2.2 times as much borrowing than the projected deficit—or a deficit less than half the size of new borrowing. It depends on whether you’re a half-insolvent or half-solvent kind of person.

One of the reasons behind the gap is accounting methodology. Loans are both a liability and an asset; just think of it like a mortgage. One borrower’s liability of $100k is an asset of $100k to the lender. In this case, the gap is driven by Crown corporations and acquiring other assets. When the GoC borrows $1 billion and lends it to a Crown corporation, it owes investors $1 billion, but it’s also owed $1 billion. The loan doesn’t increase the deficit, just interest costs and any resulting losses.

It’s debatable whether it’s a good or bad decision, but the consequences are much clearer. “Most simply, cash outlays drive borrowing, which in turn increase market debt and public debt charges, independent of how they are recorded on an accrual basis,” warns the PBO.

The PBO’s calculations show a sharp impact on public finances in the coming years.

Canada To Spend Almost 1 In 7 Dollars of Revenue On Debt Payments

The PBO warns that debt charges are now the fastest-growing public expense. Annual public debt charges are projected to climb from $24.5 billion in 2021-22 to $59.3 billion in 2026-27. Their projections show it explodes to $83.0 billion in 2030-31, much faster than revenue. The PBO estimates debt repayment will consume 13.6% of revenue by 2030-31, up from 10.5% in 2025-26. Debt servicing is set to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, consuming almost 1 in 7 dollars collected.

Most are likely to assume this is due to higher interest rates, but that’s not what the numbers show. The PBO explains that this mainly reflects a larger stock of debt, not higher interest rates. That’s the fanciest way to say the captain of this ship didn’t realize they lost their anchor.

items.title: Bet on fixed, not variable, National Bank economist tells brokers
items.description: Marion says long-end rates are near their peak and the 5-year fixed still looks attractive
items.content: <p>Marion says long-end rates are near their peak and the 5-year fixed still looks attractive</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281203142883871.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Marion says long-end rates are near their peak and the 5-year fixed still looks attractive
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

With the Bank of Canada’s October 28 rate decision, accompanied by a full Monetary Policy Report one week away, Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, has offered Canada’s mortgage brokers a direct piece of advice: recommend the five-year fixed.

Marion made the case at the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary on Wednesday, telling an audience of brokers and lenders that the country’s long-end rate cycle is approaching its ceiling — and that borrowers drifting toward shorter-term options may be underestimating the structural forces keeping rates elevated.

“It seems like mortgage holders are betting the house on short-term rates,” he said.

“In my forecast, I’d say, well, consider the 5-year rate because, you know, I think it’s attractive given what’s happening in the economy.”

His view runs against the current of the market. Variable-rate insured mortgages are running at approximately 3.79%, below the best five-year fixed insured rate of approximately 4.04%. That spread has driven a modest recovery in variable demand, with the variable-rate share climbing to 26% of the market, the first increase in three years, per a Mortgage Professionals Canada consumer survey conducted in February.

The case for caution

Marion argued the spread is misleading in the current environment. Geopolitical disruption, rising global defence spending, and an AI-driven electricity build-out are all exerting sustained upward pressure on long-term bond yields.

The Bank of Canada itself noted at its September 2 hold that “long-term bond yields have moved up globally, including in Canada” and signalled it was “prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed,” language that put an October hike back on the table. 

Marion was direct about the Bank’s October 28 decision: “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

He added that he does not expect another 100 basis points of increase in mortgage rates, and that “most of the increase that we’ve seen in interest rates is behind us.”

Why the client conversation has changed

That reading reinforces what practitioners are already hearing. Leah Zlatkin, mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in April that “most borrowers still prefer the certainty of fixed payments, especially after the sharp increases to variable rates during the Bank of Canada’s rate-hiking cycle in 2022 and 2023.”

The stakes are material. Mortgage delinquency balances rose 32% year-over-year nationally in the first quarter of 2026, and 52% in Ontario, according to Equifax Canada’s Q1 2026 Market Pulse report, a sign that renewal strain is already visible in the data.

With variable-rate market share climbing back to 26% even as delinquencies rise, broker demand and rate behaviour suggests the fixed-versus-variable conversation has rarely been more consequential.

items._ogDesc: Tariff uncertainty and surging oil prices push business inflation expectations higher in Q3 2026
items.body:
Business sentiment in Canada improved in the third quarter of 2026, but the Bank of Canada’s Business Outlook Survey (BOS) carries a harder signal for mortgage brokers.

Nearly a quarter of surveyed firms, the largest share since the question was introduced, say they cannot estimate when inflation will return to the central bank’s 2% target.

‘Too hard to say’: the new refrain on inflation

The survey, conducted between August 6 and September 2, shows the share of firms planning for a recession fell from 17% to 6%, the lowest reading since 2023. But roughly three-quarters of those interviews took place before Canada-US trade talks collapsed on August 21. Results gathered after that date show a sharp deterioration.

Claire Fan, senior economist at Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) in Toronto, summarized the shift plainly.

“Firms’ one- to two-year-ahead inflation expectations declined between May and August as oil prices and trade uncertainty moderated, but resurged in September to near spring highs as those trends reversed,” she wrote.

RBC’s analysis of the survey data puts one-year-ahead business inflation expectations at 3.7% in September, with two-year expectations rising to 3.1%.

Fan flagged the cost pass-through trend as a separate concern.

“Concerningly, half of firms surveyed — more than last quarter — plan to pass on cost increases to customers,” she wrote, noting that improved demand conditions and firms’ desire to recover margins compressed by earlier cost rounds are also driving the shift.

Canada’s annual inflation rate climbed to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August, according to Statistics Canada data released Monday — and economists say the reading gives the BoC little reason to lift its overnight rate at the October 28 meeting. https://t.co/JN1kELMQ9B — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 19, 2026

Rate decision in focus as brokers seek clarity

For brokers advising clients ahead of the BoC’s October 28 decision, the picture is uncommonly unsettled. The annual consumer price index (CPI) rose to 3.1% in September, above the prior month’s reading.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) in Canada, said the September reading keeps a hold in play.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” she said.

“Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent.”

Fan framed the broader dilemma in terms mortgage brokers will recognize. “We continue to see fragile economic recovery as the biggest counterweight to heightened inflation risks, and expect caution from the BoC, especially when rising bond yields are already tightening financial conditions and raising borrowing costs for businesses and households,” she wrote.

RBC’s base case calls for no rate hikes until 2027, but Fan acknowledged that “risks to our base case forecast of no rate hikes until 2027 are tilted toward earlier moves — including potentially as early as next week’s decision.”

items._ogDesc: A two-decade broker channel veteran takes charge of two of the bank’s largest regional markets
items.body:
BMO BrokerEdge has appointed Barbara Cook as regional vice-president for Ontario and Atlantic Canada. Cook, who previously served as the bank’s senior business development manager for Toronto West, takes charge of two of the country’s largest regional broker markets.

Cook fills a position created by the elevation of Paula Oliveira, who transitioned into a broader strategic mandate across BMO’s sales and broker program functions.

Career rooted in national broker networks

Before joining BMO BrokerEdge in April 2024, Cook spent more than four years at Mortgage Centre Canada as vice-president of franchise development and later vice-president of national sales.

Prior to that, at VERICO Canada, in her role as vice-president of national business development, she recruited more than 26 brokerage firms into the network in 2017 and a further 19 in 2018, contributing more than $2.5 billion in funded volume during her tenure.

When she spoke with CMP in a Women of Influence feature spotlighting BMO BrokerEdge’s leadership, Cook explained the thinking behind her move to the bank-owned channel:

“When I heard BMO was returning to the broker space, I thought what a great opportunity to make an impact on this side of the business, and I made the strategic move in April 2024.”

Her standing in the industry extends well beyond any single employer. Cook joined the board of Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) in October 2022 as an Ontario director, progressing through vice-chair and chair before completing her term as past chair in October 2026.

A pivotal moment for the broker channel

In announcing the appointment, Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge in Canada, pointed to the breadth of Cook’s career.

“Throughout her career, she has built a strong reputation for driving business growth, developing high-performing teams, and fostering meaningful partnerships across the broker community,” Doolittle wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Cook was direct about what she intends to bring to the role.

“I’m excited to step into my new role with BMO BrokerEdge and continue championing the growth and success of our industry. I look forward to working alongside the incredible team across Ontario and Atlantic, supporting our brokers, strengthening relationships, and building on the momentum ahead,” she said.

A multiple recipient of the CMP Women of Influence recognition between 2018 and 2025 and winner of the Women of Distinction Award at the 2020 Canadian Mortgage Awards, Cook has also been a consistent public voice for gender equity and mentorship across the broker community.

items.title: Canada’s Approved-But-Unstarted Homes Climb As Starts Slide
items.description:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) counted 143,929 homes in September that have approved building permits and no construction started.

That count, reported alongside CMHC’s figures for centres of 50,000 or more, rose 1.1% from August.

Compared with a year ago, starts have fallen. Actual housing starts in centres of 10,000 or more were down 11% year-over-year in September, at 19,984 units compared with 22,375. From January through September, those centres recorded 170,964 starts, 4% behind the same period in 2025.

“As outlined in CMHC’s latest Housing Supply Report (HSR), a key risk for Canada now is not building enough during this period of softening housing markets across the country,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC.

“Canada still faces a long-term housing supply gap and unless housing construction levels increase, improvements in housing affordability since 2023 will be difficult to sustain,” he said.

In ab Iorwerth’s view, the affordability relief since 2023 will be hard to keep without more building. Right now, starts are down from last year.

The headline figures make that harder to see: the seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of starts across Canada rose 3% in September, to 248,896 units from 242,223 in August. CMHC’s six-month trend, a moving average of that rate, barely budged, and landed at 250,411.

CMHC uses the trend alongside the monthly SAAR to account for considerable swings in the monthly figure. Multi-unit starts largely drive the market, and they can vary widely from one month to the next.

Homes already underway are holding steady. There were 371,617 units under construction in centres of 50,000 or more in September, flat from August. Completions fell 0.9% to 17,398 units.

The regional picture is uneven. “Of Canada’s four most populous provinces, only Quebec has seen modest gains in housing starts for 2026 and each of the seven major centres covered in the HSR are behind 2025’s pace for new home construction,” ab Iorwerth said.

Montreal’s six-month trend fell 8% in September on lower multi-unit starts. Vancouver’s rose 6% on higher multi-unit starts. Toronto’s was flat, with single-detached and multi-unit trends offsetting each other.

CMHC will release October’s housing starts data on November 17.

items._ogDesc: September Canadian inflation breached the BoC target at 3.1%. Regional CPI data reveals only Ontario and BC are below the national average.
items.body:
The August Consumer Price Index (CPI) report breached the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows CPI accelerated further in September. A regional breakdown reveals that only two provinces are below the national average. Headline growth is well above the BoC’s target rate, but some provinces have more than doubled that rate.

Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Already Past BoC Upper Bound

Canadian CPI annual growth.

Annual growth of CPI accelerated to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August. The outsized impact of soaring gas prices continues, with CPI ex-gasoline at just 2.2% over the same period. The agency further notes that only 3 of 8 major components saw prices accelerate too.

The headline data makes it easy to conclude this is only an energy story. However, a regional breakdown of CPI makes it clear that basket distortions are in play. Only two provinces have seen a rate lower than the national average.

Atlantic Provinces Over 2x BoC Target, Only 2 Provinces Below Average

Despite being above the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound of 3.0%, CPI may be skewed by its modelling. A quick look at the provincial breakdowns, and we see Ontario (+2.5%) is the only province below the threshold. Add BC (+3.0%) to the mix, and we get the only two provinces lower than the national average. The rest of Canada isn’t quite this lucky—especially out east.

CPI’s highest growth is almost exclusively concentrated in Atlantic Canada. PEI’s annual growth of 5.7%—approaching triple the BoC’s target of 2%—is the highest in the country. Not far behind are Nova Scotia (+5.6%), New Brunswick (+5.0%), and Newfoundland and Labrador (+4.7%). The Prairies aren’t much better off either—Manitoba (+4.4%), Alberta (+3.6%), and Saskatchewan (+3.3%) are above the national average too.

It’s not just gas, either. CPI ex-gasoline remained elevated in Nova Scotia (+4.4%), PEI (+3.9%), and New Brunswick (+3.4%). The agency separately notes “… rent prices rose the fastest in Atlantic Canada,” which can help explain some of the distortion.

Energy and Shelter Are Among The Biggest Drivers of CPI

The biggest driver of annual growth remains energy, with 19% annual growth. The sector is driven by a 27.8% surge in gas, along with a 57.8% jump in fuel oil. Considering energy is an input cost for everything, its surprising growth isn’t broad.

Shelter accelerated 1.8%, driven by home/mortgage insurance (+4.9%) and rent (+2.8%). The sector was moderated by falling replacement costs (-1.9%), tied to the cost of building new homes. It was dragged further by mortgage interest (-0.2%), which is likely to be news to brokers considering yields.

In short, Canada’s headline inflation is running hot—and the national average is weak in contrast to what most households are experiencing.

items.title: What Canada's latest inflation reading means for mortgages
items.description: Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?
items.content: <p>Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639280340084394431.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate came in at 3.1% last month, a reading that some experts believe could keep the Bank of Canada on hold when it meets next week.

The consumer price index (CPI) climbed slightly over August, according to new Statistics Canada data, but analysts including Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper say the rise likely wasn’t enough to justify an October hike.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” Cooper said this morning. “Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent.

“Still, for now, underlying inflation trends in Canada remain consistent with a patient, wait-and-see approach.”

Latest inflation reading ‘good news’: economist

A rate hold by the Bank of Canada would mean no change for variable mortgage rates, although five-year Government of Canada bond yields – which heavily influence fixed rates – have continued an unpredictable path and whipsawed over the past five days.

Those yields had ticked slightly higher at time of writing on Monday afternoon compared with the same time yesterday.

Still, National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéfane Marion, speaking in a keynote address at the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary, described the latest inflation reading as a positive one for the mortgage market.

“Good news this morning – inflation came out, it’s not dramatic,” he said. “Core inflation is still at 2%. I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

CPA Canada chief economist David-Alexandre Brassard also sees the latest reading keeping rate hikes off the table this month. “For now, there is still no clear-cut reason for the Bank of Canada to move interest rates in either direction, as both risks [a weakening economy and rising inflation] are working against one another,” Brassard said.

And he hinted that a further dramatic spike in rates looks unlikely at this stage. “I think most of the increase that we’ve seen in interest rates is behind us,” he said. “And if we’re right, it sets the stage for a normalization going into next year.”

Inflation on the rise, but sluggish economy isn’t picking up

While inflation has been ticking upwards in recent months, the economy has remained sluggish – with some forecasts indicating a further slowdown could be in store.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), which represents 103,000 small and medium-sized firms, said in its latest Main Street Quarterly report that it sees Canada’s overall GDP growth slowing again in the fourth quarter.

The latest inflation increase was spurred, unsurprisingly, by another surge in fuel oil and other fuel costs, which soared by 57.8% amid continuing price pressures from the war in Iran.

Homeowners’ home and mortgage insurance costs rose by 4.9% compared with the same time last year, while homeowners’ maintenance and repairs costs also moved higher (by 1.2%).

For now, the rate outlook remains uncertain for scores of buyers, particularly with the mortgage renewal wave still going strong.

Speaking with Canadian Mortgage Professional, Haventree Bank president and chief executive officer Fern Glowinsky (pictured below) said mortgage brokers are coming to the fore in that environment.

“I think if there’s a good option in front of the borrower right now for a longer period of time, that’s a good call,” she said. “I think if you can find an offer that lines up with affordability and structure for you that takes you through this period of uncertainty, it’s probably a good idea – because over time, things will settle down.”

items.title: Foreign homebuyer ban should be revised, says NBC’s Marion
items.description: National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high
items.content: <p>National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280326776111776.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC), has called on the federal government to revise the country’s ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers, arguing the restriction directly undermines Ottawa’s drive to restore Canada’s appeal to international investors.

Speaking at the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary on Tuesday, Marion said he expects Ottawa to act before the ban’s January 1, 2027 expiry — and that any revision should specifically permit foreign nationals to purchase new-build homes.

He framed the call around a striking market figure: 28% of newly constructed condominiums are currently unsold, a level he said is the highest since the early 1990s.

“How can you pretend to be a standout investor again if you tell foreign buyers you can’t touch the residential market in Canada?” Marion said.

“I think they’re going to revise this at a time where 28% of condos that they built are not absorbed, which is the highest proportion we’ve seen since the early 1990s. So against this backdrop, I would certainly expect to see some modification to allow foreigners to buy into new build, and that fits the overall message of making Canada investable again.”

Those views align with a growing chorus across the industry. Don Kottick, president of RE/MAX Canada, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this month that the ban has actively suppressed the very supply the market needs.

“I think if you look at the foreign buyer ban and the negative impact that it had on preconstruction, it took a lot of money out of the market that would have driven more preconstruction, more units coming on the market,” Kottick said.

“So hopefully, if that is removed in January, we start to see more investment coming back, which could drive affordability.” 

Kottick was equally direct on government intervention more broadly. “We’ve had governments that have always tried to bring policy. Policy will never fix the market,” he said.

“Hopefully the government has learned a lesson that natural market forces have been more beneficial than any government policy — because there’s always been unintended consequences.”

The remarks add a prominent voice to a debate that has gathered pace in recent months. Industry pressure for a new-build exemption has been building as the ban’s January 2027 expiry approaches, particularly among developers and pre-sale brokers.

The decision Ottawa makes before year-end ranks among the most consequential housing policy calls it faces in 2026.

Demographic slowdown and the immigration reset

Marion was equally pointed on immigration. Canada moved from roughly 1.2 million newcomers annually at its recent peak to approximately 200,000, a near-collapse in inflows that has weighed heavily on demand across Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec, where population growth has effectively stalled.

“We went from going to 1.2 million people a year a couple years ago to a dramatic slowdown, just 200,000,” he said.

“At most it’s 300,000 — that’s what the system can cope with. Negative population growth is not the solution either.”

He highlighted Canada’s long-term demographic advantage. The country remains the only jurisdiction globally projecting no population decline through 2066, a structural foundation, he argued, that underpins long-term housing demand even amid near-term disruption.

Broker implications and the 2027 stabilization forecast

Marion projected the national composite index — down 4% in 2026 — to level off by 2027, supported by labour shortages and construction cost pressures that limit the downside.

For brokers, the broader deregulation agenda Marion outlined may prove as relevant as any single housing policy shift.

“I am the most optimistic I’ve been over a decade,” he said.

items.title: Bank of Canada’s next move: what top economists are saying
items.description: Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release
items.content: <p>Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280217704442110.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release
items.body:
Four economists from Canada’s largest financial institutions are calling a Bank of Canada rate hold at the October 28 meeting in Ottawa, after September’s consumer price index (CPI) landed below market consensus and the Bank’s preferred core measures averaged 1.9% year-over-year.

The consensus is patience, but not without a dissenting voice on timing.

What economists are saying about the October 28 rate decision

Leslie Preston, Managing Director and Senior Economist at TD Economics in Canada, set the tone.

“No jump scares in Canada’s inflation in September, in contrast to higher inflation south of the border,” she wrote.

“Today’s number supports our view that the Bank of Canada can remain on hold this year. There is little evidence higher energy costs are bleeding through to broader price pressures, which remain mild.” 

Abbey Xu, economist at RBC Economics in Toronto, flagged a more cautious signal from Governor Tiff Macklem himself.

Xu noted that Macklem, speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, warned “the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has gone up,” and that the Bank has found it increasingly difficult to look through the direct impact of higher energy prices.

RBC’s base case holds the overnight rate at 2.25% through year-end before rising modestly in 2027.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC in Toronto, went further, noting that bond yields moved before Tuesday’s release on the back of Macklem’s weekend remarks.

“It’s possible that a first interest rate hike could come earlier than the January move we previously forecast,” he said. 

Dr. Sherry Cooper, Chief Economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Canada, read the September data as confirmation that energy is not yet spreading into broader price growth.

“Today’s inflation report reinforces our view that higher gasoline prices temporarily boost headline inflation while further eroding household purchasing power. However, these energy-driven increases, largely tied to geopolitical tensions, are unlikely to trigger a broader resurgence in underlying inflation,” she said.

On the Bank’s next move, Cooper was direct: “The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting. Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent. Still, for now, underlying inflation trends in Canada remain consistent with a patient, wait-and-see approach.”

Behind the September CPI numbers

Statistics Canada’s September report showed headline CPI at 3.1% year-over-year, above August’s 3.0% but below the 3.2% consensus estimate.

Gasoline prices surged 27.8% year-over-year from 22.8% in August, as crude oil reached its highest level since May.

Grocery store prices rose 1.7% year-over-year, the slowest pace since May 2024, down from 2.8% in August.

Shelter inflation ticked to 1.8% from 1.5%, driven by fuel oil costs and higher homeowners’ insurance premiums.

The Bank of Canada’s preferred core gauges — CPI-trim and CPI-median — averaged 1.9% year-over-year, slipping below August’s 2.0% and below the Bank’s own 2% inflation target.

items.title: Ahead Of BC Election, UDI, Housing Central Push For Four Actions
items.description:
On October 13, the Urban Development Institute (UDI), BC Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA), and Co-operative Housing Federation of BC (CHFBC) — the latter three of which are together known as Housing Central — published a joint news release “calling on every party in the provincial election to commit to bringing down the cost of building homes” as Election Day nears.

UDI is the group that lobbies on behalf of private developers while the Housing Central partners represent the non-profits, Indigenous housing providers, and co-ops in the community housing sector.

Because of their different focuses, the two groups are often on opposite sides of housing debates, hence why they described themselves as “unlikely allies.” They say they are coming together now because they have all reached the same conclusion: “neither sector can build at today’s costs and within an uncertain regulatory and funding environment.”

“The cost of building and financing a home in BC now exceeds what most buyers can afford to pay and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters,” the alliance said in their news release. “For market and non-market builders alike, this means projects that don't pencil and never get off the drawing board.”

With Budget 2026 earlier this year, the Province said they were adjusting the pacing of $1.4 billion in planned housing investments, which notably included an abrupt pause pertaining to the Community Housing Fund, which has stranded numerous non-profit housing projects and become a sore spot for the sector.

The groups say over 5,000 affordable rental units have been impacted, and project proponents have lost $45 million in pre-development costs.

After the Governments of Canada and Ontario announced an $8.8 billion deal this spring to cut development charges and eliminate the 13% HST on housing, the development industry in BC started pushing for a similar deal.

While the Governments of Canada and British Columbia finally made an announcement in June, it included a similar deal to cut development charges, but there was nothing on eliminating the GST, with the Province saying they were uninterested in it despite recognizing that the industry had been pushing for it.

In their joint news release, UDI and the Housing Central partners noted that the agreement to reduce development charges was not finalized before Premier David Eby called a snap election on September 22, and thus builders still cannot price it into their projects.

The alliance called for four actions to address the above points:

  1. Restoring the planned investments into non-profit, co-op and Indigenous housing so that the development of 5,000 affordable homes can get back on track.
  2. Finalize a commitment to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market and provide housing stability for thousands of tenants across BC.
  3. Finalizing the federal-provincial agreement on development cost charges and infrastructure within [90] days of forming government, so DCC reductions reach projects on the ground.
  4. Following Ontario’s lead by securing a GST exemption on new homes for all buyers, not only first-time buyers.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said BCNPHA CEO Jill Atkey. “The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” added UDI CEO Mike Drummond.

Housing has not been as front-and-centre compared to the election in 2024, with this election’s primary focuses being Eby’s record and decision to call the election, the economy, and BC’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).

The most substantial commitment on the housing front has been Eby and the NDP’s proposed Unsold Condo Tax on completed unsold inventory, which has drawn widespread criticism from the industry.

Election Day is Saturday, October 24.

items.title: September CPI keeps Bank of Canada hold in play
items.description: Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline
items.content: <p>Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280143870576555.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate climbed to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August, according to Statistics Canada data released Monday — and economists say the reading gives the Bank of Canada (BoC) little reason to lift its overnight rate at the October 28 meeting.

Energy drove nearly all of the acceleration. Gasoline prices surged 27.8% year over year, up from 22.8% in August, as crude oil reached its highest level since May amid ongoing Middle East conflict.

Broader energy costs rose 19.0% annually, following a 15.4% gain the prior month. Excluding energy entirely, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose just 2.2%.

Core pressures stay contained

For mortgage brokers advising clients on rate timing, the more instructive signal came from the BoC’s preferred core measures.

CPI-median fell to 1.9% in September from 2.0% in August, while CPI-trim eased to 1.8% from 1.9%, both moving away from hike territory and averaging 1.9% across the two, down from 2.0% the month prior.

Leslie Preston, managing director and senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, offered a clear verdict.

“No jump scares in Canada’s inflation in September,” she said.

“There is little evidence higher energy costs are bleeding through to broader price pressures, which remain mild. Today’s number supports our view that the Bank of Canada can remain on hold this year.”

That view aligns with analysis from Abbey Xu, economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, who found limited evidence that elevated energy costs were generating significant second-round inflation in her reading of August’s data, a conclusion September’s numbers do nothing to challenge.

Grocery prices also moderated further. Food purchased from stores rose 1.7% year over year in September, the smallest annual gain since May 2024, down from 2.8% in August.

Shelter prices edged up 1.8%, with rent rising 2.8%.

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

What October 28 means for brokers

The September CPI release is the last major data point before the October 28 decision, which will be accompanied by a full Monetary Policy Report.

As CMP reported following Canada’s September labour market shock, a deteriorating jobs picture had already pulled near-term hike expectations sharply lower.

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union in Edmonton, described the Governing Council’s bind plainly.

“We believe it will opt for patience,” he said.

“As a result, we think the BoC will keep its policy rate unchanged for the rest of the year, unless there are signs in the CPI data of a broadening of inflation.”

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Vancouver, pointed directly to Monday’s release: “The Bank of Canada will likely hold off on a rate hike, especially if the inflation data released on October 19 brings no nasty surprises.”

With the overnight rate at 2.25%, held across eight consecutive meetings, mortgage professionals navigating client conversations ahead of the October 28 BoC decision now have their clearest signal yet.

As Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, has cautioned: “There’s no clear signal that rates are heading materially lower, and in some cases we’re already seeing lenders adjust pricing upward.” October 28 looks unlikely to change that.
